speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subtopic: TABLING OF CANADIAN REPLY TO PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on December 16 the Minister of Public Works tabled the text of a letter dated December 13 which had been addressed to me by the chairman of the council of ministers of the Soviet union, Mr. Bulganin. I should now like to table the text of the Canadian reply, which was given to the Soviet ambassador on the evening of Saturday, January 18, for delivery to Mr. Bulganin.
As the house is aware, similar letters were addressed in early December to the heads of governments of other NATO countries. These other NATO countries are also in the process of replying. The United States reply was delivered on January 12, the French reply on January 14 and the United Kingdom reply on January 16.
The Canadian government, in the reply I intend to table, deals essentially with the first letter and acknowledges receipt of the second, although some of the same points appear in both letters. As I said in the house on January 13, it is our intention to give further consideration to Mr. Bulganin's second letter, the one dated January 8, and to consult in the NATO council with regard to the issues with which it deals.
What the NATO countries looked for in these letters was evidence that the Soviet union was sincere in its expressed desire to adopt measures leading to the improvement of the international situation and to the creation of the necessary confidence in relations between states. We found little that was new in the letters, although it was recognized that they were more moderate in tone than Soviet communications received in the past. Also they placed emphasis on the settlement of differences by negotiation, an objective which certainly finds support in this and other countries. It was with these considerations in mind that the NATO governments examined the letters and agreed on the general nature of the replies to be given.
96698-225J
In preparing the Canadian reply the government has tried to adopt as positive an attitude as possible. We wish to reduce tension and to help settle world problems, but the need still exists-and this must be emphasized-for a strong defence system. In a positive sense, the reply displays our continued willingness, within the terms of a disarmament agreement, to open all or part of Canada to aerial and ground inspection on the basis of reciprocity. This type of proposal should prove mutually attractive to Canada and the U.S.S.R. since they are neighbours across the Arctic. Mr. Bulganin is reminded of Canada's strong interest in disarmament, and it is suggested that since he advocates step by step progress in this field the first step should be for the countries concerned to resume their discussions and to make use of the United Nations machinery created for this purpose.
In the reply we say that we intend to join with our NATO allies in studying the comments made by Mr. Bulganin on a proposal put forward earlier by Poland for the creation of a zone in central Europe free of nuclear armaments.
The assertion is made in Mr. Bulganin's letter that a meeting of heads of capitalist and socialist countries on a high level could have great significance. As I mentioned in the house early last week, this observation is made more specific in the second letter, the one dated January 8, with the proposal that a high level meeting be held within the next two or three months. Our reply states that a meeting at a high level would receive the Canadian government's support if there were adequate assurance that beneficial results could be expected, and if the utmost care were given to its preparation.
While on the subject of a possible summit meeting I might refer to the reply I gave in the house on January 7 in response to a question asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie, as to whether or not Canada would consider issuing an invitation for a summit meeting in Canada. As I said then, we attach great importance to reopening negotiations and would agree to examine any proposal which might result in the reaching of an agreement between the Soviet union and the western countries. In my reply to Mr. Bulganin I referred to the interest that had been displayed in this house in the possibility of a high level meeting, and I said that when the participants

Inquiries of the Ministry decide that they are ready to call such a meeting and should they decide to hold it in Canada, situated as we are between the United States of America and the U.S.S.R., such would be acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, yesterday at the request of the hon. member for Gloucester I gave a figure for the number of registrations at unemployment insurance offices across Canada. The figure was 796,000.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a great deal of misrepresentation of that figure. Despite the fact that I emphasized that this figure has never been accepted as an official unemployment figure, there is still a tendency to consider it in that light. In the

Globe and Mail of this morning, for example, the figure is referred to as "796,371 jobless."
I make this point, Mr. Speaker, because a number of members have asked me about the figure, and I want to point out that it was not the policy of the previous government to release it. In fact on numerous occasions members of the previous government made it very plain that the only official unemployment figure was the dominion bureau of statistics figure, which now stands at 386,000. It has a serious effect on public confidence, Mr. Speaker, when a figure which is in fact an operational figure relating to operations of the unemployment insurance commission is persistently referred to as the official unemployment figure.
This government is not responsible for the two sets of figures, nor is it responsible for the stand that the dominion bureau of statistics figure is the only unemployment figure. This was the stand taken by the previous government; and since they established the figures, they should know. I wish hon. members opposite would give the dominion bureau of statistics figure the same ready acceptance they did when they sat on this side. I shall continue-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I promised the hon. member for Charlotte that I would make a statement today regarding coastguard service provided in Canada. Since this same question has been asked by a number of members and there seems to be considerable interest in it, perhaps I might be excused for making a full statement on this matter.
With perhaps two important exceptions, both of which are covered by other government agencies, the substantial fleet of vessels maintained by the Department of Transport as part of its marine service activities performs the same functions as those of the United States coastguard and, indeed, a great many additional functions. United States coastguard activities are devoted in large part to provision and maintenance of buoys, lights and other floating and fixed aids to navigation, and the supply of isolated stations
Inquiries of the Ministry such as lighthouses. They also provide some icebreaking and related navigational assistance.
The Department of Transport maintains a fleet of over 30 vessels, located on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts and in the St. Lawrence and great lakes areas, which also perform these functions, as well as concentrating on coastal icebreaking work and major convoy and navigational assistance in the Arctic areas during the summer season. We have built and are building a number of excellent new vessels to satisfy this requirement.
The department's vessels do not undertake police patrol activities, nor have we any desire to enter the policing field. This function is carried out very effectively by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who also have a number of special cutters operating on both coasts and in the great lakes for this purpose.
Usually references to a coastguard are connected with marine search and rescue, since this is a field in which the United States coastguard receives, from time to time, considerable publicity. In the United States the coastguard has been charged with a major role in the field of search and rescue generally, and performs tasks of search and rescue in coastal areas both for air and marine purposes. Its activities in this field are based largely upon the maintenance and operation of a very substantial fleet of specialized aircraft, supplemented as well, where the need arises, by its coastal vessels.
In Canada this function is performed by the Department of National Defence through the Royal Canadian Air Force, which has followed generally the same course as the United States coastguard in developing specialized aircraft and personnel to assist in the matter of search and rescue, in fact on an even broader basis than in the United States because the Royal Canadian Air Force, in its operations, covers not only coastal areas but inland territory as well.
Moreover, the R.C.A.F. search and rescue keeps in touch with various vessels operated by the various government departments, as well as private vessels, so that in co-ordination of marine activities they are in a position to carry out the same function as the United States coastguard.
To provide a fleet of special vessels solely for marine search and rescue work in Canadian waters would be a large and expensive undertaking-

These are available to assist in marine search and rescue work in their respective areas, along with the ships operated by the Department of Fisheries and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: FISHERIES
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF SMELT NETS UNDER INSURANCE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my absence from the house on Wednesday last the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi directed a question to the house leader respecting the inclusion of smelt nets under the fishermen's insurance plan.
The interdepartmental committee, comprising members of the Department of Fisheries, Department of Finance and the then department of resources and northern development, which studied the question of fishermen's insurance in 1953, recommended confining insurance to vessels and lobster traps.
Circumstances which would militate against the inclusion of other types of gear are as follows: (a) the short life of nets; (b) the difficulties of identification; (c) the fact that many nets are repaired from year to year and thus are made up of materials of varying ages; (d) the assumption that the loss of nets was considered less serious than the loss of a vessel, in that replacements would be more easily financed, and (e) the difficulty of differentiating between wear and tear and accidental damage.
Continued demands for insurance of nets have come repeatedly from the smelt fishing areas of New Brunswick and the cod trap areas of Newfoundland. In these two fisheries it is true that the net is a much more significant item of equipment than in most other fisheries, and serious losses are rather frequent.

Suggested Resignation of Government
Suggestions have been put forward from time to time concerning means which might overcome the problem, but I am sorry to report that no practical means has yet been suggested which would allow the inclusion of fishing nets under the insurance scheme. However, my department is giving the problem continued careful study.

AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
At ten
o'clock last night, Mr. Speaker, I had just begun to deal with some of the things the government had failed to do. You will recall, however, that I did give them credit for having taken a number of steps to create work as a means of alleviating unemployment in this country. I must also give them credit for at least making an effort to stimulate trade with Britain and perhaps other parts of the commonwealth, and I sincerely
hope their efforts and their zeal will result in greatly expanded trade between these countries and Canada.
At the same time I must say it has been hard for me to understand the attitude of the government with regard to the acceptance of sterling, particularly, and the currencies of other countries in return for Canadian goods. The Social Credit group in this house first began to advocate the acceptance of sterling as far back as 1945, at the time of the Bretton Woods debate. We have continued to advocate it since then as one means of trying to overcome the stagnation of trade caused by the Bretton Woods agreement. We pointed out at the time that the Bretton Woods agreement would unquestionably result in stagnation, and we have continued to take the same stand ever since.
We moved an amendment in 1952 calling for the acceptance of sterling and every member in this house, with the exception of the Social Crediters and six Conservative members, voted against our motion. Amongst those who supported our motion was the present Prime Minister. That was one of the reasons I felt I could not understand the continued refusal of the government to accept local currencies, particularly sterling, as a means of stimulating trade.
I mentioned last evening that the government failed to bring in a budget. I would suggest that was a most serious omission, because by bringing in a budget at this session it would have been possible for the government to provide for the financing of various projects designed to prevent the downward trend which had its beginnings during the time of the Liberal administration, and to prevent unemployment from developing into a first class depression.
I also suggested last night that one of the things that could have been done and probably should have been done was to budget for a deficit so that government investment could take the place of declining private investment, as was suggested, by inference, by the Leader of the Opposition, at least until normal conditions returned. By a deficit budget I simply mean planning to spend more than is taken from the people in the form of taxation and other revenues. I realize, of course, that the government persists in its adherence to orthodox financial practices and therefore, as long as it does, budgeting for a deficit would mean increasing the national debt.
A good look at the statistical review of the Bank of Canada, the most recent issue, will show that the interest on our national debt has been going up year by year until it now is approximately half a billion dollars a year.

Suggested Resignation of Government If we had in this country a Social Credit administration, budgeting for a deficit would mean asking the Bank of Canada to make available to the treasury the amount of the budget in excess of the expected revenues, which new money would be used by the government for public investment in exactly the same way as if that money had been taxed from the people or borrowed from the banks. The big difference between our proposal and the orthodox one would be that under the Social Credit proposal the amount of the deficit would not add to the interest-bearing debt of the country. The government has failed to come seriously to grips with the tight money policy so as to prevent the downward trend from seriously increasing unemployment and trade stagnation.
In agriculture the government gives every indication of knowing the problem but does not appear to know what the answer is. The price support legislation they brought in is little, if any, better than the price support legislation the Liberals put on the statute books back in 1944. Under the Conservative bill the grain producers of western Canada have been completely ignored and neglected, even though they form one of the most important sections of the agricultural industry. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the government has thus far shown an inclination to let emotional and political considerations influence them to do things that have deepened the stagnation in the oil and gas industry.
I point out these things because I think the Conservative party should realize that they have no good reason to be spoiling for a fight. They have a lot of things to do yet before they can be certain that if there is an election they will come back into office with even as many members as they have now. Mr. Speaker, I realize that they have not had time to do everything, but I must say they will have to settle down seriously to face these problems that harass the people, and quit merely tinkering with things.
What is our position with regard to the amendment and the subamendment? We believe this is not the time for foolish political manoeuvring. The world situation and our internal economic difficulties are too serious to be throwing the country into confusion just now. We do not believe that anybody in this house is justified in putting party above the welfare of the people as a whole. We should be seriously pooling our knowledge and our abilities in the wider interests of our country. We thought when the people spoke last June they had made it clear that they wanted their new government to have a reasonable chance to show what they could do. Seven months is not enough time for that purpose, especially When those seven months


includes the difficult months of winter when any soft spots in the economy show up with startling magnification.
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I have conducted ourselves all through this session as if we believed what I have just said. Now the Leader of the Opposition is asking the government to resign and give over the reins of government to the Liberal party without an election. As I think about that I remember how indifferent the Liberals were on several occasions to high unemployment during wintertime. They claimed it was seasonal and regional and temporary.
Those terms-seasonal, regional and temporary

have been so burned into my conscience that I shall never forget them. When I bear in mind the fact that it was either policies instituted by that party or things they left undone which started this country into stagnation and carried it before last June 10 quite a way down that road; when I think of the tragic decline in farm cash income during the past six years; and when I add to these things the fact that the Liberal party got as far out of touch with the people of Canada as they did, I find it difficult to see for Canadians any advantage whatsoever in a change of government at this time from Conservative to Liberal.
I have not seen since June 10 any evidence of repentance on the part of the Liberal party, or any change of heart which would give me confidence that they realize how wrong were many of their policies. I think what they need is a sufficient time for quiet meditation in the political wilderness to bring their hearts and souls once more into tune with the desires and the will of the people of Canada before they seriously ask for the right once more to govern this country.
Under these circumstances I cannot with any conscience vote for their amendment. I have a strong feeling they will be relieved to hear that I will not disappoint them.
And now, Mr. Speaker, a word about the C.C.F. subamendment. There are some things in it that we could support. However, the final lines are couched in such terms as to indicate clearly that the means they would propose using to try to solve the unemployment and economic situation in our country would be socialist methods. We have no quarrel with their holding these views, but of course we cannot support them, and therefore we must vote against the subamendment. The rules prevent us from moving a second subamendment. If it were not so we would move one.
And now, Mr. Speaker, a final word to the government. I said they have been

spoiling for a fight. There has been altogether too much of this business of daring people to take a stand lest it serve to bring on an election. I think they ought to stop that sort of thing. I think they ought to get down to business and show the country that they have confidence in themselves. When they talk about asking for dissolution, or asking for a defeat in this house so they can go to the country in an election now when there is serious unemployment, when there is a serious business decline and uncertainty, when there is general stagnation, they are indicating to the people that they lack confidence in themselves, that they are afraid to stay on the ship and try to bring it safely into harbour.
If they are really and earnestly concerned about finding a solution to these problems they will not want an election now. They will realize that it is irresponsible to talk about an election under these circumstances. The thing for responsible government to do, whether in a minority or not, is to stay at the wheel and use all the ability and imagination they possess to find and give effect to honest and complete solutions to the problems the Canadian people face.
Just one final word. The two combatants in the big debate yesterday stood toe to toe and emasculated one another with truth; but in that debate they demonstrated that both their parties were iron men with feet of clay. All they proved was that what is needed is a new concept, a new approach to things economic and financial in our country. It is clear that neither of the historic parties has the answer to the business cycle, that is the alternate periods of boom and bust that so frequently follow one another across the pages of our economic history. Both of them should move over, when the time is right, and let someone who has the answer tackle the job.

Mr. Speaker, before I deal with the substantive part of my remarks I should like first of all to give to the house the attitude of the official opposition with reference to the amendment to the amendment moved by the C.C.F. party. Speaking on behalf of the official opposition and dealing with the amendment to the amendment, I should say first of all that it is a substitution and not an amendment. I should like also to say on its substance that much of it is a repetition of our own views, with the exception of the words which occur toward the end of the resolution which read:
-by adopting a fiscal policy which will enable the government to redirect investment and embark on a comprehensive program of public development.
Suggested Resignation of Government
It is this part of the amendment to the amendment that raises some doubt in my mind, and I am sure in the minds of hon. gentlemen in the house who do not belong to the socialist party, that it may well mean the socialization and control of banking and finance; and if it does mean that then it seems to be a denial of the principles of free enterprise for which we on this side of the house stand.
In addition to that, sir, the amendment to the amendment strikes out the operative and substantive parts contained in the last two paragraphs of the amendment moved by my leader. For those three reasons I therefore say that it will not be possible for us to vote for and support this amendment, but on the contrary we will vote against it.
I rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to support the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. My first words in so doing are to commend and congratulate him not only for a fighting speech but for a constructive, effective and devastating speech so far as the policies of the present government are concerned. Just as I was proud to call the former leader of the opposition my leader, because as has been said on all sides of the house he was and is not only a gentleman of the highest order but also a great statesman, so also am I happy and proud to call the new Leader of the Opposition my leader; and I, together with those who sit with me on this side of the house, will be loyal to him in every respect.
I referred to the effective and constructive speech which he made, coming as he did from a convention assembled here in this city the like of which has never been seen at any time in the history of this country. Coming from that convention as he did fortified with a forward looking program he was able to deal with the weaknesses and inefficiency of the policies of the government. In contrast two and one half hours were taken by the Prime Minister to deal with the 50 minute speech which my leader made. And then, notwithstanding the two and one half hours taken by the Prime Minister yesterday to deal the remarks of my leader, it must be remembered that he had one week at 24 Sussex street or at his own office in which to prepare his speech.

A little later on he said:
Some people for reasons best known to them are gloating over unemployment and rubbing their hands with unholy glee with every increase in unemployment, however seasonal it may be.
Listen to this.
This is no time for gloom. It is a time for a realistic appraisal of the facts.
Could there have been a gloomier speech than that delivered by the Prime Minister yesterday?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT

It is surprising that the Prime Minister would not have seen or not have known about the statement made by the Minister of Finance at that time. And when all this was done, had the government seen the secret report when the Minister of Finance stated in his alleged baby budget speech of December 6, to be found at page 2003 of Hansard, that he accepted Mr. Harris' forecast of revenues? Surely the Minister of Finance knows that revenues would fall if economic conditions deteriorated.
If the government had seen the report of last March in November why did the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance try to
[Mr. Chevrier.1

conceal its contents from the public and give the optimistic statements which both of them did? Even if they had not seen it surely they had got more up-to-date estimates in the five months before the Prime Minister spoke on "The Nation's Business", and surely they had got them from the same economists as had prepared the document from which I read earlier.
On what then did the Prime Minister base his statement of November 9 that unemployment was not generally serious? If unemployment was not generally serious, as he stated, then based on these reports the position has changed and substantially deteriorated now. Did he just make up the statement or was he advised that such was the case? Was he not relying on the same economists who prepared the March forecast? The March forecast is now past history. Past history will not help the unemployed because, as the position is today, what people are interested in knowing is what is the government doing now, in January of 1958, to meet the position and the facts as we find them?
But even the Prime Minister's history is wrong because the March forecast was succeeded by a mid-year forecast published at the time the government took office. I should like to quote now from a document prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1957, Mid-year Beview." If the Prime Minister had only gone forward to June instead of going back to March he would have found that the forecast by the economists was more optimistic. I should like to quote from two paragraphs of this 1957 mid-year review where I find the following:
The June survey of capital expenditure intentions of Canadian business, institutions, governments and housebuilders, reveals that aggregate spending intentions have been revised moderately upward from those outlined at the beginning of the year.
Farther down the same page I find the following:
The somewhat better outlook for house building reflects the improvement in housing starts that has taken place in recent months and the expectation that further improvements will occur as the year progresses.

speechtext:
As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has said, it does seem like seven lean years.
However, they have been in office for seven months. We were given the impression, during the campaign and since, that when they would take office the Tory government would get rid of all sorts of difficulties about which they had complained when on this side. We would see a wonderful new era, the like of which had never been seen in this country before. What we have been experiencing instead has been more like a cold shower than a wonderful new era.
We should like to know something, too, on this side of the house about Conservative policies; about their program which has been one which we are unable to discern, certainly from their convention and still less from what has been given to us in the house. I could refer, of course, to the trade proposal to divert $600 million of imports from the United States to the United Kingdom. But if this is a policy, it seems one far more difficult to implement than those who enunciated it in the beginning believed. Notwithstanding the trade mission to the United Kingdom, there is no evidence yet that the government can divert any trade. There is no evidence yet that even a fraction of the 15 per cent can be diverted.
This proposal has caused embarrassment to both the United Kingdom and Canada. The United Kingdom has countered with a free trade proposal about which the government will tell us nothing. Export trade, as my leader has said, is important to the economy of Canada. The diversion of trade rather than expansion is at the back of the seriousness of the unemployment situation. The Prime Minister in his speech dealt at great length with the excellent statement delivered by my leader last July in San Francisco. The Leader of the Opposition said what he and other Liberals including the Right Hon. C. D. Howe had said before in the United States, that the lack of a balance of trade should be corrected. The diagnosis of the problem is the same as the Tory diagnosis. After all, the facts are the same and the facts are there. But the solutions to the problem are exactly opposite. The Tory way is to restrict and divert imports from the United States and thereby reduce trade. The Liberal way is to get more exports into the United States thereby expanding trade.
Then there is, sir, the all important subject of federal-provincial relations. When I flashed the blue book a moment ago I could have read at considerable length from some

In the middle of September the Prime Minister wrote the provincial premiers inviting them to come to Ottawa to deal with the questions arising out of federal-provincial relations. He had stated before that if he took office he would call a new federal-provincial conference in order to deal with fiscal matters.

No, it was not done. My hon. friend says, "That was done." It was not done by any stretch of the imagination. What was called was a preliminary conference and the subject of fiscal relations was never dealt with, as this house well knows. It will not be dealt with before the next election.
It was stated also that the necessary measures would be taken to have municipal governments represented at this conference. Municipal governments were not represented at the conference by either invitation from the Prime Minister or any other means. It was stated also that the government would adopt an attitude conducive to decentralization, and more particularly apply to the provinces a more advantageous fiscal arrangement. Instead of decentralizing, as had been promised, there has been more centralization because one of the measures brought down in this house by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) is clearly one indicative of centralization.
Finally, in calculating the federal contribution to the hospitalization plan, the intention was to include the costs of mental illness and tuberculosis. This was not done. I could go on and deal at length with the promises made in so far as the conference was concerned. The letter of the Prime Minister in September, which was an invitation, the letter of the Prime Minister of October 31, which veered from the position as originally announced, and the speech of the Prime Minister at the conference, which was considerably at variance with what had been promised and with what was contained in the letters, then the press release and the letter written by the premier of Manitoba, all lead one to the conclusion that there were only three results from the conference.
These three conclusions were, first, that in the last few months the Conservative government had violated or refused to fulfil election promises that had been made in the field of federal-provincial relations. It is clear now that fiscal arrangements will not be revised, as I said a moment ago, before the next federal election. Next, the federal government invited the provincial premiers to come to Ottawa under false pretenses. The


federal government, which had promised to treat the provinces with deference and without arrogance, succeeded in doing what no other federal government up to this time had dared to do and that is, at the last moment, without advising the provinces beforehand, completely changing the agenda of the conference, afterwards imposing that agenda upon the conference notwithstanding the protests of several provincial premiers.
Finally, the conference concluded with no practical results in so far as a solution of that pressing problem in connection with federal-provincial relations is concerned, namely fiscal arrangements. From that point of view, as stated recently by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill), it was nothing more than another Mont Tremblant.

In today's dangerous world Canada's need is for a closer drawing together of all the elements in Canadian society into a strong and vital national consciousness that respects the various cultures upon which Canadian society is founded.
