speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I open my remarks this afternoon by extending, as a onetime student to my one-time lecturer in English constitutional history, my warm congratulations on his election last Thursday as leader of the liberal party and Leader of the Opposition. May I also say it is a pleasure indeed to follow in this debate a former classmate, and to see sitting near him, evidently awaiting impetuously for an opportunity to participate in this debate, another former classmate, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). Times have changed in the space of 30-odd years and I can only attribute what has happened to my hon. friends to the fact that they have been keeping bad political company.
The hon. member for Laurier this afternoon did his best to repair the irreparable damage done yesterday. I am sure the hon. member for Essex East, when his turn comes, will make a gallant effort, but the breach made yesterday cannot be repaired. It is too wide to be repaired by the efforts of even these worthy orators. My hon. friend from Laurier sought this afternoon to saddle some steeds to his purpose, but I am afraid those steeds are tearing him and his party apart today. And, Mr. Speaker, all of Chev's horses and all of Paul's men won't put Mike together again.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: A sense of humour at last.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The shambles in which the opposition was left yesterday at the conclusion of the memorable and masterly speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) were certainly not of the creation of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), and I am sure that in whatever he may do to try to repair the breach we will give him credit


for gallantry today. I am quite sure also that he would not have planned the first two days in this way.
Mr. Speaker, the noise we have heard here yesterday and today indicates that hon. gentlemen opposite are smarting under chastisement, not merely the chastisement inflicted by the Prime Minister but also the chastisement of their own consciences when they compare what they have been trying to do this week with the bold heroics of last week.
Then, Mr. Speaker, they were as bold as brass. Why should not they? Then the supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite were told that there would be a restoration of normal opposition if a certain course was followed. Is this an example of normal opposition, the abnormal course of action proposed yesterday by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson)? Last Thursday night great emphasis was laid on the word "soon". I well remember that it was added at the end of a pause, and how it brought on the cheers. Evidently, we learn now that "soon" does not mean "soon"; it means "some other time". It is to be a case of opposition if necessary, but not necessarily opposition. If our friends opposite have entered what might be called a fighting ring, with the echoes of last Thursday night's cheers ringing in their ears, then it is evident that what was said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) yesterday amounts to saying they will fight in only one-half of the ring and that there will be at least three neutral corners. They are all for democracy, Mr. Speaker, but not for elections. Away with the ballot box, is their cry. This is the party which once boasted about trusting the people. They will do anything, Mr. Speaker, rather than face the people now.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Why don't you try it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we ever get them to the ballot boxes it will only be by dint of dragging them, kicking and screaming to the polls.
In the situation which was faced yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition it seems to me that the courses open to him were simple. The choice between them might not have been simple, but the courses open were simple. It was a case of choosing between a courageous course and what might be called, in the language of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), a course of discretion. Had the hon. member taken the course of courage he would have come out with an uncompromising challenge to the government and, win, lose or draw, people would have admired him, whether they were his supporters or not, because people like a fighter.
The other course, the course of discretion, would have involved the hon. gentleman in

taking, in effect, the attitude that while he might talk about bold and imaginative courses he was not in a position, if he were to be frank with the house, to take a bold and imaginative course, and had chosen rather to run away to fight another day. I wish to say in all seriousness to the Leader of the Opposition that I think he would have come out of this, his baptism of fire as leader of his party in this house, with a great deal more credit if he had followed either of those courses rather than the course he did follow. The one which would have gained for him the greatest measure of respect would have been the course of courage, in the light of the words which he and his supporters used at the convention last week.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) can boast about the convention. It is not a convention that we are witnessing now; it is the shambles of the Liberals in opposition in this house. "I was not told to win or lose", said Laurier after the defeat of 1911, "my orders are to fight". The orders of the Liberal party today are not what they were in Laurier's day.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Exactly the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Speaker, if the orders are the same the orders are not being obeyed today.
The Leader of the Opposition chose to follow neither the course of courage nor the course of discretion. He made the worst of both worlds. He chose to contrive a pretence of leading an opposition. He was, he sought to convey to us, bold as brass, but he contrived his pretence in such a way that his amendment could not be supported by other parties. And so, instead of going down like a fighting man, the Leader of the Opposition has led his followers into ignominy following yesterday's sham. The heroics of last Thursday faded out on Monday. The atomic-powered new leadership fizzled. The bomb proved a dud. The new Liberalism that was boasted of last week exposed itself as the same musty old Liberalism disguised by a change in the style of ties. Discredited and defeated at the polls it remains.
If only the delegates at this convention last week could have been here yesterday to see the Liberal members of this house bedraggled, beaten, forlorn and looking thoroughly sick.
The hon. member for Laurier was at pains to assure us this afternoon that the Liberals did not like the speech the Prime Minister made yesterday. Mr. Speaker, we did not need to be told that. It was written right across every face opposite; they were an ill-looking official opposition.
Suggested Resignation of Government
What is the picture which the hon. gentleman sought to portray? It was something like this: on June 21 everything was all right in Canada up to 11 o'clock that morning; and ever since everything has been all wrong.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
And if there is not going to be a recession brought about by other means, they will not be happy until they have created a synthetic recession in Canada.
They have talked about trade, and said that trade is deteriorating. The fact is that our exports are up in 1957. The figures are available up to the end of the 11 months, and they show that for the first 11 months of 1957 our exports were higher than during the first 11 months of 1956. Why do not hon. gentlemen opposite either inform themselves or learn to give the people facts, not fiction?
Now, as to imports. Imports for the first 11 months are about the same as for the 11 months of last year. They are down slightly. But hon. members opposite will not have forgotten that the virtue of external trade, as measured by them, is not to be found in the figures of export trade. Times without number they have told us that the virtue of trade lies in import trade, and that a big import trade is an index of prosperity. Their concern, evidently, is not that our exports have been increasing but that our imports have declined slightly.
We are not worried as a government as a result of a reduction in the record trade deficit that this country was incurring under the trade policies of the former government, deficits mounting year by year to record proportions until last year they amounted to $850 million with the world and $1,250 million with the United States alone, which broke all records. And so we say that the time has come to apply policies of expansion of trade in other directions as well.
We have drawn attention to the fact that it has been, if not Liberal policy at least the outcome of Liberal policy to put Canada's trade eggs in one basket and so the extent to which Canada's trade balance has been directed in one channel by the policies of the former government has been the occasion of warning comment year after year by those of us who sat yonder in the seats of the opposition. The extent of that channelling and the increase year by year have run to these figures: 74 per cent of all Canada's imports have been coming from the United States; 60 per cent of all Canada's exports have been going to the United States, and two-thirds of the trade Canada does with the world has

Suggested Resignation of Government been done with the United States. Mr. Speaker, has this never given cause for concern to hon. gentlemen opposite?
It is interesting to note that it evidently gave concern to one of their colleagues who is no longer with them, the former minister of national revenue, Dr. J. J. McCann, who is quoted in the Toronto Globe and Mail as having said on September 12, 1952, when the extent of the channelling and when the putting of the trade eggs in one basket had not gone nearly so far as it has since under the policy of the former government:
"Canada's economic position, at present strong, also has a weakness," revenue minister McCann told the National Tax Association at its 45th annual conference in the Royal York hotel yesterday.
"That weakness is that Canada depends so much on the United States," said Dr. McCann. "Canadians can never be freed from the fear of a slump in the United States, for which we would not in any way be responsible and which we could do little to control."
That was the picture in 1952. It suited the political conceptions of hon. gentlemen opposite to watch that trend go forward and make no attempt to prevent that channelling growing to that extent. They ignored the loss of trade with the United Kingdom and with the commonwealth and it remained for this government under the distinguished, courageous and vigorous leadership of the Prime Minister to set about repairing the wrongs and the harm that Liberal policy had done to Canada. The thing that hurts hon. gentlemen opposite is that we are on the way to succeeding in expanding trade with the United Kingdom without hurting trade with other countries one iota.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Is there to be no diversion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite
choose to deride this effort. When my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) led a distinguished Canadian trade mission to the United Kingdom and accomplished in that mission the greatest success that has ever been accomplished by any trade mission that has ever gone from Canada's shores, did he receive any recognition or credit from hon. gentlemen opposite? They chose to ridicule instead. We know that they never were interested in commonwealth trade or in making the commonwealth more effective. It is better known today than it ever was before that at commonwealth prime ministers' conferences for many a year in the days of the former government Canada dragged its feet at those conferences.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We did not put British proposals under the table.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
What a refreshing fact it is, Mr. Speaker, that now Canada is taking an active part in the commonwealth and is

pulling her fair share of the load in an attempt to make that commonwealth effective for the good of all parts of the commonwealth. However, hon. gentlemen opposite are not content with our aim to expand commonwealth trade without hurting Canada's trade with any other country. Instead of being satisfied with that they have been indulging in the most crass form of misrepresentation for some time.
I want to say a word about oil. Hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to make it appear-and I do not need to remind you of the things they have been saying in this house and at their convention-that the steps taken by the United States to restrict imports of Canadian oil were taken as retaliation against the trade policy of the present government. I have only three things to say about those assertions. The first is that they are false.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Prove it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The second is that it is a base calumny upon the administration of the United States. The third is that in making statements of that kind they are, to their own knowledge, weakening the hands of the Canadian government in supporting Canada's interests in these present negotiations. The course of action adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite has been as irresponsible as anything in the history of the Liberal party.
In regard to this matter of expanding trade with the commonwealth, let me remind hon. members in the face of the misrepresentation by the Liberals on this score that there has been no forcing attempted by this government, that there has been no cutting off of United States imports except that we took steps to apply import controls to protect the Canadian agricultural producer of turkeys, fowl and skim milk in order to safeguard the price support system that had been set up in this country. Do hon. members opposite criticize us for the steps we took to protect the Canadian agriculturist against imports of turkeys, fowl and skim milk? If so, let them have the courage to declare that position.
In the midst of all their misrepresentation in regard to trade relations with the United Kingdom, let me remind hon. members opposite that this government has initiated something that they either said was impossible or did not even try to bring about, the holding of a commonwealth trade and economic conference which will be held in Canada this year and at which every proposal that any member of the commonwealth wishes to bring forward will be brought forward and discussed-

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: And treated like the Thor-neycroft proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
-at the proper time and place.
I have this concluding word to say on the subject of trade relationships with the United States. I do not need to go over the ground again that was covered by my leader in his devastating speech last night. I simply comment that the day after the Leader of the Opposition made his speech in San Francisco in July 1957 the Montreal Star made an interesting editorial comment on that speech which sounded like a very challenging speech delivered for United States ears. I do not think anyone will pretend that the Montreal Star has had a bias in favour of the Conservative party or the present government but in its editorial columns, July 17, 1957 issue, the Star said of Mr. Pearson's speech:
He would never have said that while he was in office, for he was cutting near to the bone.
And then, these are the concluding words of the editorial:
Mr. Pearson has done a good job for Mr. Diefenbaker.
Mr. Speaker, we shall not forget the brave words that issued from Mr. Hellyer, the former associate minister of national defence at the Liberal convention last week when he called for a tougher policy toward the United States. Our policy, as was so clearly stated yesterday by the Prime Minister, is to stand up for Canada's interests under all circumstances. It is regrettable that when we came into office Canada was still suffering in its trade relations with the United States from the failure and neglect of the former government to put Canada's position fairly and squarely before the United States administration.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: "We fixed 'em."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: In the face of their feeble protests over the United States agricultural surplus disposal program and the other ways in which action had been taken at Washington that hurt Canada's trade we had to go in and put before the representatives of the United States government the true attitude of Canada on these subjects and believe me we had little to work on in the way of representations made on these subjects by the former government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hence oil restrictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say this? On the subject of United States investment in Canada, which we have encouraged, which we have invited, we have had to overcome the handicap of misrepresentation of our position in this respect by the former government and its supporters. We found that their misrepresentation of our position in this respect had found its way down there, and we have had to devote our efforts to
Suggested. Resignation of Government undoing the miserable work that the misrepresentation of the Liberals had done to Canada's position in this respect.
If hon. members opposite want a very good exposition of the kind of position that we have been setting forth in this matter, I refer them to two speeches which were never made in Canada but are quite worth reading today. They are the speeches made by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, one in Chicago on October 15, 1956, and the other in Milwaukee on October 16, 1956, when he reminded the United States that Canada is not a state of the American union.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the next subject on which there has been misrepresentation on the part of the Liberals, and that is the subject of unemployment. First of all I want to speak about employment. Do you realize, that employment in Canada reached an all-time peak in August, 1957? Do you realize that since this government came into office in June, that in June, 1957, there were more people employed in Canada than had ever been employed in any June in Canada's history? Do you realize that in the month of July, 1957, there were more people employed in Canada than had ever been employed in any July in all of Canada's history? Do you realize that in the month of August, 1957 there were more people employed in Canada than had every been employed in any month in Canada's history? Do you realize that in the month of September there were more people employed in Canada than had ever been employed in any September in Canada's history; the same thing in October; the same thing in November and the same thing in December. The latest figures on employment show that there were more people employed in Canada in December, 1957, than had ever been employed in Canada in any December in our history.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Not in December.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Not in December.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East cannot change the figures or the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: He will try to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Let us, having reminded
ourselves of the figures of employment, seek to measure the extent of unemployment. Unemployment is something, whenever it raises its head, that must give any patriotic and responsible Canadian concern. Let there be no doubt in anyone's mind that the unemployment that does exist and has existed has

Suggested. Resignation of Government commanded the deep concern of the government in our efforts, and continuing efforts, to grapple successfully with it.
But in the face of all the misrepresentation as to the extent of this problem, let us look at the facts. The unemployment in Canada today is not what hon. members opposite have been saying in this house and outside. It is not the figure given to the Liberal convention last Wednesday night and last Thursday night by the present Leader of the Opposition or the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). It is not the figure of 796,000. That is the figure of registrations with the unemployment insurance commission and they well know that, and they know, as well, if they will face the facts, that the figures of registrations with the unemployment insurance commission have been swollen as a result of legislation passed by this parliament, the bringing of fishermen within the scope of unemployment insurance, the extension of more benefits to married women, the extension of the seasonal unemployment benefits in recent days under legislation introduced by the present government in the present parliament. All of these factors have had the effect of increasing the number of registrations, not to mention the fact that in 1957 the Canadian labour force increased by four per cent, the biggest increase in the Canadian labour force in all our history, as compared with an increase of only 1.9 per cent as an average for the five previous years.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Why didn't you cut down
immigration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Let us examine the extent
of unemployment, and examine it as a percentage of the labour force. The total of unemployment, as we have it from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) in his statement yesterday, is 386,000 at mid-December. That happens to be 6.5 per cent of the civilian labour force. Let me compare that with some of the figures of recent times so that we see this problem in perspective. Let us go back no farther than 1955. In January, 1955, what was the percentage of unemployment then? It was 6.8 per cent; in February, 1955, it was 7 per cent; in March, 1955, it was 7.4 per cent. Did hon. members opposite then say that there was a great and serious unemployment problem? No. They were hiding their heads in the sand and denying the existence of any unemployment problem at all. Those of us who were in the house at that time will not forget their tactics.
If you want to take it as a percentage of those registrations with the unemployment insurance commission then you have figures that are swollen and inaccurate in their size.

But if they will compare those with the figures for the same months that I have compared with the December, 1957 figures, they will see precisely the same results, that the percentage of unemployment today is less than it was three years ago. That is not enough. Hon. members of the official opposition, as I indicated earlier, are seeking by every means at their disposal to create the psychological ingredients of depression, and they are doing it for petty partisan advantage.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
What about the Prime
Minister's speech last night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We will not forget the way in which they have rubbed their hands in unholy glee over every increase in the figures of unemployed. It does not matter that these reveal the extent to which Canadians have been hurt as long as they of the opposition achieve some mean, partisan advantage. It cannot be denied where the responsibility must rest. The fact is, sir, that the Prime Minister has so devastated the sham, so penetrated the pretence of hon. members opposite and their party, that little needs to be added on this subject. The fact is that in the face of the storm warnings that were made evident to them in March, 1957, they ignored them, they neglected them, they concealed the facts. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, I go farther than the Prime Minister did last night. The Prime Minister said last night that the former government had concealed the true state of affairs, the gathering portents of economic deterioration. But on March 14, 1957, the then minister of finance, speaking for the government, went a stage farther and he said:
I come now to consider the economic prospects for the coming fiscal year. On the present evidence I think we can expect a continuation of the current high level of economic activity throughout the coming year.
It was not enough that they concealed the advice that they were receiving from competent sources, Mr. Speaker; it was not enough that they tried to conceal from parliament and from the public the facts, that they had due warning that unless steps were taken, then Canada was in for some economic troubles; no, they went farther and from the mouth of the minister of finance we had this statement that all is well. Mr. Speaker, they have been not only improvident, not only neglectful, but they have misrepresented the facts to the Canadian people and for that they will certainly be called to account.
On this subject of responsibility, and the efforts of hon. members opposite to exculpate themselves from responsibility that is theirs, let me read to you what has been said by a gentleman who, in his editorials, can never

be accused of being Conservative. He is regarded as a Liberal. This is Bruce Hutchison writing an editorial on November 30.
It is difficult to understand why a statesman of Mr. Martin's brilliance should insult the public mind by blaming the Diefenbaker government for a slight deflation in an inflationary boom. This simply won't stick. For obviously if any change in the economic climate stems out of government policy at all, it stems out of the policies that have gone before.
They were the policies of hon. members opposite. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition himself was much more frank on this subject before he assumed his present office because you will remember that just a month ago when he was asked about his views on this subject he made some comment. This is what he said at Quebec, as reported in the Globe and Mail of December 28:
Lester B. Pearson and Paul Martin, contenders for the leadership of the Liberal party at its national convention at Ottawa next month, said here today the Conservative government cannot altogether be blamed for the current economic slow down and rise in unemployment.
And further:
For his part Mr. Pearson said: "I think it would be a big mistake if we blamed the government for the unemployment of the last months."
Those were true words, Mr. Speaker, but what will you say now of the language used by the hon. gentleman yesterday and at the Liberal convention last week in seeking to saddle responsibility on the present government for a situation that it inherited from its neglectful predecessors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Why don't you do something about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I want to say this. We have taken and will continue to take measures to grapple with the problem of unemployment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: What measures?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Where are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We have sought to get to the heart of the problem by contributing to the prosperity of the farmers of the west through cash advances on farm-stored wheat, by getting rid of Canadian wheat through the efforts of my hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by economic development in the maritime provinces, by unemployment insurance benefit increases, by unemployment assistance provided in a way that the former government refused to do, by tremendous amounts of money made available to stimulate house construction and by government construction proceeding at other levels.
Let me make it abundantly clear to every member of the house-I made this clear
Suggested Resignation of Government in the financial statement I made in the house on December 6-that the instructions that have been given by the government are to the effect that while we are seeking to reduce expenditure where expenditure is needless we have said that there shall be no reduction in expenditure where it means jobs, and we are seeking to increase construction in useful public works down the line. While next year we would unquestionably like to have a balanced budget, let me make it abundantly clear that we are not going to put a balanced budget above our firm determination to provide, through the agency of public works, jobs for unemployed Canadians.
The Leader of the Opposition undertook to deplore the fact that I had not brought in a budget. What he really means, Mr. Speaker, is that he is not satisfied with the budget that was brought in by the former minister of finance on March 14 last, for that is the budget under which we have been operating and if there is anything wrong in the budgeting the fault lies with that budget. We never promised to bring in a budget at the fall session.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: You did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
All that was said was that steps would be taken to fulfil the promises made. Those steps have been taken, those promises have been fulfilled, and we are going to go on with the same task, with the same quest, in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer and in the interests of the well-being of the Canadian economy.
Do you realize Mr. Speaker, that if the Liberals had been re-elected on June 10 there would not have been any financial statement last fall? The fact is that the house has more information today as a result of the complete financial statement made in the house on December 6 than it would have had if there had not been a change of government. The house would not have had any statement but for the change of government. And, Mr. Speaker, when they say that revenues are falling let me tell the Leader of the Opposition that revenues up to the sixth day of January in the present fiscal year, covering more than the first nine months, are $92 million ahead of what they were in the same period of the previous fiscal year.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: How about December?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, any tool will serve the purpose of hon. gentlemen opposite as long as they succeed in destroying confidence, and in trying to destroy confidence in the government they will not hesitate and they are not hesitating to destroy, if necessary, confidence in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Smoke and fury.

Suggested Resignation of Government

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Let me make it abundantly clear that as a government we will take every needed step within the means at our disposal to meet the problem of unemployment. Let me say that hon. gentlemen opposite need not think that democracy in this country and in this house is going to exist half and half. It is going to be complete democracy, not democracy without the ballot box. If they will have the courage of their convictions, the courage to challenge the government, then let me make it clear that we have no fear of those who are the supreme judges in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Bring it on then.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hold it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says "bring it on". Mr. Speaker, it is all very well for hon. members to say that. Some of them have been saying it but they are just saying it in undertones. They are afraid to hear themselves say it. Let them come out of their holes and shout it from the housetops. Let them stand up in their places and say it. Let them challenge us, Mr. Speaker, because we stand in our places in this house prepared to meet any challenge.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to deal specifically with the subamendment we have presented to the house because I know there are many Liberal members who would like to vote for that subamendment. Many of them have told me so and in view of the statements of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) a short while ago I want to dissect the subamendment and show to my Liberal friends that they can safely support it without doing violence to their Liberal convictions.
It has been suggested that this is a doctrinaire socialist subamendment but I find in it no mention of a publicly owned banking system; no mention of the public ownership of public utilities, which many Liberals who came to their convention last week from my district were in favour of; no suggestion that the vast monopolistic corporations that now dominate our society should be taken out of private hands; none of the things which in our view are necessary if we are going to have a permanent and stable economy.
What we did present here was a suggestion for immediate action to deal with the economic crisis with which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) dealt at such inordinate length yesterday. We are merely suggesting certain measures that could be taken. The first of them is the question of considering the proposals of the United Kingdom. Are the Liberals afraid to vote in favour

of that? I would call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that on January 7 the present Leader of the Opposition who was not then leader of the opposition had this to say as recorded at page 2970 of Hansard when he was pinned down very firmly by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) as to what his attitude would be toward these trade proposals. He said this:
But, Mr. Speaker, I will be very glad indeed to tell my hon. friends what I would have done in the matter. I would have announced at once that this is a far-reaching, imaginative and constructive proposal on the part of the United Kingdom government and one which seems to indicate the seriousness of their intention of getting closer economically to Canada, something which my hon. friends have often talked about, and I would have followed that up by saying that this proposal should be immediately and sympathetically considered in discussions between the two governments.
So it would appear, Mr. Speaker, that there is nothing to prevent the Liberal party from supporting that part of our subamendment. It has been suggested to me that the part to which they take exception, the part they hesitate to support, is the final phrase in which we say:
-and also for consideration of immediate action to relieve unemployment and distress by adopting a fiscal policy which will enable the government to re-direct investment and embark on a comprehensive program of public development.
Are my hon. friends in the Liberal party opposed to a program of public development? If so, Mr. Speaker, how do they explain the monotonous regularity with which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) reiterated again and again his plea that this government should embark on a program of public investment in Newfoundland similar to the one in which they are engaged in the other maritime provinces? If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is in favour of public investment in his adopted province, is he not in favour of a similar program in other provinces? We should know that, because the other provinces will be very interested in knowing. If he is in favour, and if his colleagues in the Liberal party are in favour of a public investment program all across Canada, how do they propose to accomplish that without decisive changes in fiscal policy?
It is not long ago-in fact I believe it was yesterday-that the Leader of the Opposition was denouncing the government and deploring-quite rightly-the fact the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had not introduced a budget this session. He went on to say this as recorded at page 3518 of Hansard for January 20, 1958:
We do not know very much about the national budgetary picture. We do know that expenditures have not been reduced as promised, but

vastly increased. We do know that the course of national production has been levelled off and is probably declining, that revenues are declining, that there will almost certainly be a deficit in the present fiscal year and that there is a prospect of a huge deficit in 1958 to 1959.
If the Leader of the Opposition seriously considers that the Minister of Finance is sitting like Mother Hubbard in front of a cupboard that is bare at the moment, and at the same time he and his party are in favour of a program of public investment across Canada, how do they propose it shall be instituted except by changes in fiscal policy? That is all we have asked for in our subamendment. It would have been easy for us to have introduced into this house an amendment couched in such terms that the Liberal party could not possibly have accepted it.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That was their trick.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That was their trick. We could have followed an even cheaper trick, similar to theirs, by taking from their statements one or two phrases that have been uttered in this house or at that splendid convention or even incorporated a resolution adopted by the Liberals, and put the Liberal party on the hook. We decided that the situation that was debated at such extraordinary length yesterday by the leaders of these two parties is really of such a serious nature that no responsible group in this house should introduce an amendment unless it contained some positive, substantive proposal for dealing with the problem.
I would suggest that the Liberal party could quite easily support this amendment. I could promise them, in the future, they would have every opportunity they wished to vote against socialist amendments in this chamber. At the present time, all we are suggesting is that a certain course should be followed. It may, and I say only "may", deal effectively for the time being with this serious economic crisis. I put it to my Liberal friends that that would be a reasonable course for them to follow. I would suggest to them also that they had better be quick about following such a suggestion because even the Tory government embarked on a certain measure of re-direction of investment in this country when they announced the additional sums to be provided for housing, and when the other day the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) told us that if it becomes necessary the government will provide further funds. These facts, taken in conjunction with the gloomy statement of two weeks ago that the minister saw no prospect of funds for housing coming from traditional, orthodox sources, would indicate that this 96698-226
Suggested Resignation of Government government is determined to take at least one faltering step towards the re-direction of investment, with of course apprehensive glances over their shoulder at those shadowy but powerful figures that lurk behind both Liberal and Conservative parties. Nevertheless, the government is taking a few hesitant steps. Are the Liberals afraid to take similar steps?
I would suggest also, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment of ours offers the Liberal party a further opportunity perhaps to retrieve something from the disaster that overwhelmed them yesterday. Do not make any mistake about it, it was a disaster that overwhelmed them. Crowds came to this chamber yesterday expecting to see drama, perhaps even melodrama, and they were given farce.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: They were, given low farce.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yes, low farce. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I thought when the Leader of the Opposition was preparing to introduce his amendment, judging from his rather giggling, simpering manner of producing it, that he was going to play a joke on the House of Commons. I thought this was a merry jest. Then I found he was serious and he actually moved it. As I say, it was farce-no, it was not only farce but it was tragedy, deep tragedy, the extent of which will not be known for some time. It is a tragedy that a once great party comes to this house and has the effrontery to suggest, after having been thrown out neck and crop through the front door, that they should be allowed to creep in through the back door. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I never thought to live to see the day when a responsible political party in Canada would suggest that we should adopt the political styles and customs of South American countries. This is Venezuelan politics, where governments change office without benefit of the opinion of the electorate. I should add also that even Adolf Hitler, when he first came to power, came via the ballot box. But not these gentlemen!
I have been told that the Leader of the Opposition can lay claim to some standing as an historian. I have been informed also he has at least one other colleague who can lay some claim to being historian. I am not a historian, but I do remember some of the past history of the Liberal party. I am afraid that the Leader of the Opposition has not studied the history of his own party or his memory could take him back as mine takes me back to 1926, when on June 25 the Liberal party was defeated in this chamber. On
3572	HOUSE OF
Suggested Resignation of Government June 28 the then prime minister Mr. Mackenzie King tendered his resignation to the governor general, after having been denied the right of dissolution.
On the 28th, the same day, Mr. Arthur Meighen of the Conservative party took over the reins in this chamber. He lasted for four days and he was then defeated. The house was dissolved and an election campaign ensued in which the then leader of the Liberal party fought the election campaign almost entirely on the basis of the unconstitutional action by which he had been deprived of the right of dissolution. Now today we have these gentlemen seriously- at least we must assume they are serious- coming before this chamber and asking us to re-enact that drama only to have the roles cast differently and the outcome to be entirely different.
It would be quite amusing if it were not tragic because, as I said before, it was a tragic thing we saw yesterday. In fact I thought when I witnessed it of that Shakespearean tag, "Let us sit on the ground and tell sad stories of the death of kings"-even newly-crowned kings. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there was never such a short period elapse between a coronation and an abdication.
I am in a Shakespearean mood today and I came across another quotation which is to be found in Act III of "King John". It says:
Thou ever strong upon the stronger side!
Thou fortune's champion, that dost never fight
But when her humorous ladyship is hy
To teach thee safety!
Yes, it was a rather tragic scene we witnessed yesterday. We saw something else that was not very pretty to behold; we saw a magnificent hatchet job done on the Liberal opposition in this house and, as one who on occasion can use a fairly sharp machete myself, I give the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) full marks for a magnificent hatchet job.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
You
had better hold your applause.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
And yet I wonder if that is the role which the Prime Minister of Canada should play. I wonder if he should have rushed with such relish into the abattoir. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I wondered when I heard the Prime Minister speaking whether he really supports the bill placed on the order paper by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). When I saw him bring whole batteries of rhetoric, whole arsenals of guided missiles of vitriol and invective in order to shoot one forlorn sitting duck-a sitting duck, indeed,


already crippled with a self-inflicted wound- I wondered if the Prime Minister really believes in the humane slaughter of animals.
However, there is this to be said: those who employ cheap shoddy and dishonest arguments cannot complain if their antagonists are not too choice in their selection of weapons and not too scrupulous in their use of their methods. When I read the acceptance speech of the hon. Leader of the Opposition I found him saying "What is the situation now; after seven months of a Conservative government in office, unemployment rising to the highest level since recorded figures were taken". When I heard him speaking of the serious condition of our external trade and relating that condition to the first paragraph in which he mentioned the period of seven months of the Conservatives' in office, I felt such tactics were not worthy of the leader of a great party in this country. I say this because he knows, or if he does not he should know, that the train of events which has created our present discontents was already set in motion before he and his colleagues left office.
I know quite well that later on he said that it would, of course, be unfair to blame the government for all these things, but he created the impression-and I am unable to believe he did not intend to create that impression-that there is an automatic link between a Conservative government being in office and a high level of unemployment-fantastic suggestion that because one set of incompetents was thrown out of office to make room for another set of incompetents, then certain economic events have taken place.
While I say I deplored, coming from the Prime Minister of Canada, a savage and brutal attack such as he made yesterday, on the other hand I was unable to have too much sympathy with its victim because when he speaks of trade in this house and suggests that because the Prime Minister made some rather free-wheeling and perhaps indiscreet suggestions about diversion of trade to the United Kingdom that created our difficulties with the United States, he was again stating something which he knows, or ought to know, is not presenting the facts as they are. I commend him to the remarks of Sir Saville Garner, the British high commissioner, as reported on the radio this morning when Sir Saville was speaking of trade with the United Kingdom. He spoke of the ties of sentiment which link us with the United Kingdom but he said that trade is not a matter of sentiment, trade is hardheaded business.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I would suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that the businessmen of

the United States are just as hardheaded as those of the United Kingdom and that if they see it is to their advantage to buy our oil, our base metals or any other of our basic commodities, they will do so and they will do so no matter whether the Prime Minister himself were to preside at a burning in effigy of Mr. Dulles in front of the parliament buildings and, conversely, if they do not wish to buy from us they will not do so despite the most honeyed phrases in the best diplomatic tradition.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, was not a very happy day for this parliament. I think both the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister can be very thankful that their performances yesterday were not exposed to the pitiless gaze of the public as was the great Liberal convention last week.
What did we have yesterday? We had the Prime Minister blaming the Liberals and the Liberals blaming the government and I was reminded when I listened to it of a rather amusing incident which took place many years ago in the legislature of British Columbia. We had in our group at that time a very witty and intelligent member who one day after she had listened to the premier and the leader of the opposition in that parliament engage in the sort of nonsense that we got from these two gentlemen yesterday in this chamber, rose to speak and said, "You know that reminds me of two nasty little boys confronted with a broken window; one says, 'You done it', and the other one says, 'You done it', when they both know in the bottom of their nasty little hearts that they both done it."
The Prime Minister was so busy reminding us of something of which no informed person needed to be reminded, because we are all well aware that the economy was on the down grade before June 10-in fact we were warned so recently as February of last year by the governor of the Bank of Canada-the Prime Minister was so anxious to remind us of that fact, that he forgot one thing. He forgot to tell us what he intends to do about it. Perhaps that is not fair, Mr. Speaker, because I do believe we are going to have a vast program of picnic grounds which to me, incidentally, bears rather an ominous sound because I recall that in the hungry thirties that is what we did in British Columbia. We put the unemployed, or some of them, to work making picnic grounds.
But the Prime Minister did not get around to telling us what he proposes to do any more than the Liberal convention or the Leader of the Opposition got around to telling us. We heard quite a lot about the infanticide of political ideas at the convention and everybody cheered it as a remarkably clever 96698-226i
Suggested Resignation of Government phrase. The Liberal party is, of course, a modern, progressive party and it does not believe in infanticide. It believes in birth control, and it made quite sure that no new ideas came to birth at that convention which might have to be strangled later on. Any ideas that might have come out of the "grass" were scarcely encouraged; the "grass" to which the "brass" was going to get so close, and it did, as close as the lawnmower gets to the grass that it rolls flat. This rejuvenated Liberal party did not tell us what it was going to do, either.
But if bold policies are to come from the Liberal party I would suggest-and I almost hesitate to say this today-that they may have to come from no less a place than the head of the Leader of the Opposition, and I want to recall to your mind, Mr. Speaker, an interchange between that hon. gentleman and myself which took place on November 27th, 1957 and which is recorded at page 1594 of Hansard. I had been referring to, and very rashly attempting to paraphrase, a report of a speech which the hon. gentleman had made some time earlier, and I said:
I refer to the hon. member for Algoma East. It was a speech made shortly after the arrival of sputnik No. 1 on the horizon. During it he made this remark-and he will correct me if I have it incorrectly-or said something to this effect, that it now appears obvious that our social and economic organizations did not fit us to keep pace with the Russians. He qualified that statement later by saying that of course, even though it did not fit us to keep pace with the Russians, it was much to be preferred to that of the Russians and was much superior. It struck me, however, as a rather hopeful sign that a gentleman of his eminence should be prepared now in public to state that perhaps the time has come for a serious overhaul of our economic and social organization.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend tell me when I am supposed to have made those strange
observations?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I must apologize for not being able to do so because I did not clip out the article. But I will get it for the hon. member. I will admit that I was very much surprised to read it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
So am I.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that you will recall those words "these strange observations". It took me some time to find this speech but finally I got it, and I do not think it is confidential. I may say it was a speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition, before he was elevated to that dignity, at the University of Minnesota on November 3 and he entitled his speech "Where do we go from here?" I wonder if that was prophetic. The part to which I refer, and to which he took exception, and which he stigmatized as "strange observations", is to be found on page 5 of his manuscript, and in order not to be accused of misquoting him by reading out of
3574	HOUSE OF
Suggested Resignation of Government context, I am going to read the whole of the paragraph preceding the one I paraphrased:
What do we oppose to this controlled and centralized society? Too often, merely the well-worn cliches of the superiority of freedom and democracy and our "way of life". I don't want to be misunderstood. These things are superior to anything that Soviet communism can produce or will produce. The imposed order and the directed activity of the Russians may seem to give them at times a selective advantage over our free and competitive society, but in the long run there is no salvation, no hope, in their system because it enslaves the free thought and free soul of man to the dictates of a few irresponsible despots.
I imagine there is no one in this chamber who would quarrel with any of those words. But the hon. gentleman went on to say this:
While that "long run", however, is taking place, there are some signs that our own social and economic and political institutions will not be equal to the challenges which face them; that these cliches which I have mentioned are too empty of content for too many.
They were not too empty of content for the 5,000 Liberals who came to the coliseum last week. It is quite true that I used the expression "obvious" instead of "some signs" and that I did make specific reference to the Russians, but I assume that the hon. gentleman included the Russians among the challenges which face us. And if these remarks are strange-I do not think so; I think they are quite hopeful-in fact this is the only hope I have left for the Liberal party-then perhaps the leader of that party will yet come forward with some constructive ideas, and will yet decide to lead his party in the spirit of that document.
I was astonished that the hon. member should have stigmatized those remarks or rather my rough paraphrase of them, as being strange observations. He can, maybe, find some way of avoiding doing anything about them, but I should like to ask him this: what does he think now? Does he still think that our social and political and economic institutions require some reorganization? Does he still have doubts as to whether they will fit us to meet the challenges before us, and, if he still has those doubts, how does he propose to change them and in what form? I think the people of Canada are entitled to know that today. It was not very important what the hon. member for Algoma East said in Minnesota, but it is very important today what the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition is prepared to say in this chamber.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: He should have said it in his amendment yesterday.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I am not sure whether we should go back to that sad afternoon. It strikes me as a tragedy in the vein of Greek tragedy in which by an inexorable process


the fates overtake those who display the qualities of heart and mind that invite the fates.
Yesterday we were discussing elections, and I did some figuring and came to the conclusion that the next election I fight- and it seems this will not be too far away- will be the eleventh, counting by-elections and general elections. During this career I have faced more defeats than victories but out of this harsh and bitter school of experience I have been able to find a few small nuggets of wisdom for politicians- and I use the word "politicians" in this sense: a politician, to my mind, is a member of a profession which is the very core of our democratic process-and the chief nugget of wisdom I have found in the course of that very chequered career is that there is one defect which a politician cannot possibly have and hope to survive, and that is the defect of irresoluteness. And I could not help thinking yesterday that the Leader of the Opposition must have wished he had a Lady MacBeth beside him to whisper in his ear: "Infirm of purpose, give me the dagger".
Now what are those gentlemen going to do? What are those two naughty boys with their broken window going to do? I am going to suggest to both of them that the Canadian people will not be interested in whether the decline in our economy took place after June 11 or whether it had begun before that date. They want to know what is going to be done today. You are now being faced with a problem which you have been avoiding for 20 years. Now let us see you make it work.
You will not make it work by adopting the role of Pollyanna. As a matter of fact, I am surprised how Pollyanna hops back and forth across this chamber. Or, perhaps more correctly, Pollyanna always sits on the government side of the house but a different person takes her role. The Minister of Finance this afternoon was speaking the lines of his predecessor in the role of Pollyanna. One of his colleagues, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) was out in my part of the world not long ago where he made a speech which is reported in the Vancouver Sun of January 16, 1958, under the heading, "Living in Fool's Paradise". The article reads in part:
Lumbermen Rap Hees for Rosy Industry Forecast
Transport Minister Hees needs a new crystal ball, in the opinion of British Columbia forest industry leaders.
Mr. Hees, in an address to the Truck Loggers' Association Wednesday, forecast higher sales of Canadian lumber and wood pulp at home and abroad in 1958.

Suggested Resignation of Government
He said the lumber industry can expect a better year in 1958, and that in the case of wood pulp there appears to be more opportunities for increased sales.
He added that many of the obstacles faced by exporters have been, or are being, removed and no new major adverse developments have appeared.
It was the rosiest outlook painted for British Columbia's number one industry in many months and the reaction of industry officials was fast and irate.
"The minister appears to have been misinformed," said Ralph Shaw, president of MacMillan and Bloedel.
"The situation we face is so serious that we should be aware of it and act accordingly. Living in a fool's paradise of unfounded optimism could get us into serious trouble."
"We only wish Mr. Hees' forecasts were true but our economists warn us that 1958 will be a year of continuing adverse results for us," said Peter Sinclair, head of Crown Zellerbach Canada.
M. J. Foley, president of Powell River Company, said provided the pulp and paper industry remained competitive and could keep costs down, there might be some minor improvements this year, but he added:
"There is no such present indication."
These gentlemen who are now in office are as blithely optimistic as the gentlemen they put out of office last June. Neither of these parties has come up with any positive, concrete program for dealing with this severe economic crisis which, as I said yesterday, was dealt with at such intolerable length by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister. The Canadian people will not be satisfied with words in this chamber. The Canadian public wants to know what you people are going to do and if they do not like what you are doing then I trust they will be given an opportunity to choose between you when our Liberal friends seek, as I hope they will, to repair some of the damage they suffered yesterday by voting for the eminently moderate and carefully thought-out subamendment which we have placed before this house.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every hon. member of this house regardless of with which party he is associated will readily understand how I feel when I say in my first words since the election of the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) to the leadership of the Liberal party that I join with all my colleagues in the Liberal party in pledging him my support, loyalty and faith in his capacity to make a great contribution to our party and to the public life of Canada.
I venture to suggest that it is no extravagant utterance for one associated as I have been with the hon. member for such a long period to say that his career both as a public servant, as a member of this house, as a former president of the United Nations and as one of the world's most distinguished
figures makes him the kind of man who surely, whatever may be our political conviction, would cause us all to recognize as a future Prime Minister of Canada. I am sure that what I have said thus far will find agreement in every quarter of this house; but I venture to express the view now, speaking as an obvious partisan, that he will become prime minister much sooner than most hon. members in this house think.
It must be obvious that the statement made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition really did hit home because it provoked the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to make the longest speech -1 have ever heard him make in the course of 12 or 14 years in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: And the best.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: From the point of view of debate one of his best, but from the point of view of content one of his worst. The speech made by my leader was one that obviously disturbed the Prime Minister but it also disturbed my hon. friends sitting down to my immediate left in the far corner of the house, as well as the leader of the Social Credit party. By the way, I want to acknowledge at once to that party my deep appreciation for their foregoing their opportunity to speak at this moment in order to give me the opportunity of participating in this debate.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman suggests that we were foregoing our opportunity to speak at this time. I wish to point out that we are doing nothing of the sort. We receive only one opportunity to speak out of every six opportunities. It would be the normal opportunity for a Liberal to speak at this time and not a member of this party.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I did not want to embarrass my hon. friend in any way. I understood from the whip that that was the situation. My hon. friend, I am sure, will understand that I did not say that with any malice whatsoever.
It is obvious that the speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition is one that greatly disturbed the Prime Minister because that hon. gentleman not only attacked the views of the Leader of the Opposition but he also attacked his courage. Although he did not attack his integrity he came pretty close to the kind of body blow which, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat said, one would never have expected particularly on an occasion like yesterday to have been launched by the Queen's first minister in this country and in this house.

speechtext:
Your leader asked for it.

The statement made by the Leader of the Opposition is one which, having in mind all the circumstances, undoubtedly marks him as a man of the greatest capacity both in opposition and ultimately to establish the right for himself to sit immediately opposite in the seat now occupied by the Prime Minister.
I should have thought that the occasion yesterday was one on which the Prime Minister, recognizing the necessary importance that we must all attach to world affairs at this time and to the easing of the international tension, would have taken the cue from his Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) who when sworn into office said he hoped he could see develop in this country a bi-partisan foreign policy. I would have thought that yesterday the Prime Minister, recognizing the prominent qualities of the Leader of the Opposition as one of the great figures among those men and women who have worked for peace in our time-

You have had great experience in these matters and just as you, when you were secretary of state for external affairs, collaborated on the traditionally generous scale with the former leader of the opposition I, as Prime Minister, particularly now that you have been elected to the leadership of the largest opposing group in this house, will seek to take advantage of collaborating with you in trying to make a common contribution toward the promotion of a satisfactory and constructive foreign policy in Canada".
I should have thought that is what he would do, but no, we did not have that kind of offer from the Prime Minister who generally I have found to be a rather understanding and generous man even though a very formidable opponent. I would have thought that yesterday, taking advantage of the greatness of this occasion, the kind of occasion in which he loves to participate, he would have said: I recognize that although we are opponents we have in foreign policy a minimum of differences. I recognize your experience and I would like from time to time to collaborate with you in our foreign policy. But no, what did the Prime Minister do? He at once, early in his speech, first by

speechtext:
We are here at this time to discuss two amendments directed against this government and one of them calls the government's attention to something which this government will not be allowed to escape from, namely its responsibility in the matter of unemployment in this country.
We have been told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) that there are almost
800,000	individuals who have applied for unemployment insurance. We were told by him yesterday that as of mid-December there were 386,000 men out of work. I am sorry the minister is not in his seat.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: He is here.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I am glad he is. I am sure the minister will not deny what I am going to say. By the time he received the last report the number of jobless in this country was close to 500,000, and the number of individuals who are now applicants for unemployment insurance is away above the figure of 800,000.
The Minister of Finance spoke a moment ago, and in speaking of this situation he tried to minimize it. He said that the working force was greater now than at any time before in Canadian history. I said that was not true in the month of December. I want to point out what I meant when I interjected. In the month of December last there were 5,061,000 individuals in our working
force working 35 hours a week or more. Excuse me, that was December, 1956. As of December, 1957, there were 4,887,000 men in our working force working 35 hours or more a week. To point out that because the working force is greater today as an excuse for there being 700,000 to 800,000 men and women applicants for unemployment insurance and close to 500,000 men out of work is to give an explanation that does not in any way relieve the kind of suffering that attends any one man who is out of work, no matter who is responsible, which government, which party or which situation. The fact is that this government cannot escape the fact that we now have unemployment at the highest level at this time of the year as compared with any other period, higher than since 1933. These are the facts that cannot be overlooked.
As an indication of the seriousness of this matter, I find, for instance, that in September, 1956, unemployment insurance benefits paid out amounted to $7 million in round figures; in 1957 for the same month the figure was $13,786,000. In October of 1956, $8 million was paid out compared with $16 million in October of last year. In November of 1956, $9 million was paid out compared with $18 million, in November, 1957. In January of 1956 the figure was $33 million representing the amount paid out, and it is estimated that this month there will come out of the unemployment insurance fund $63 million. It is estimated that in February $69 million will be paid compared with $38 million in the same month of 1956. As for the month of March I have seen the estimate made that $72 million will be paid out compared with $44 million in March, 1956.

remind you of what you said when you were sitting on this side of the house and just as you charged us with responsibility then, we charge you now as the head of the government that you should do something about this problem.

Here is what the Prime Minister said on his way home after the NATO meeting, after his famous television broadcast in which he gave us such an intimate and detailed account of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization summit meeting. Here is what he said to the reporter in Winnipeg:
The government "has acted and will continue to act" to meet the current unemployment problem.
What were the figures then? What has the government done to meet the current unemployment problem?

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Speeches.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister had another idea when he was on the opposition side. He said to the government of the day headed by the right hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. St. Laurent), "I will


tell you one way to cure this problem; call the provinces together, let us have a conference, let us discuss this problem." I say to the Prime Minister, and I am going to quote his words in a few minutes, that that sounds to me like a pretty good idea, particularly when we are confronted with the greatest unemployment level we have had since the last Tory government in 1935.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: As a result of your policies.

maintopic: AMENDMENT CALLING FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I say that sounds like a good idea. Why does the Prime Minister not call the provinces together? If he calls them together he can have a double purpose in mind. He can do something, as he promised he would, about fiscal relations and he can also take advantage of their presence in Ottawa to discuss unemployment in accordance with his suggestion in 1955 that the provinces should be called together. What the Prime Minister said in that connection, when addressing himself to an amendment respecting unemployment, is found in Hansard of March 15, 1955, at page 2039. This is the present Prime Minister speaking, the then hon. member for Prince Albert. He was not leader of the opposition then. If he had been, possibly he would have chosen his words a little more carefully. However, here is what the Prime Minister said to the former prime minister who is now sitting next to the Leader of the Opposition:
The people are asking for a promise of action. Will the Prime Minister not assure the Canadian people that he believes action is necessary and that when this conference-
The conference about which I spoke.
-meets in three, four or five weeks, one of the first things to which this conference will give consideration is the problem of unemployment?
