Mr. Speaker, the economic wealth of a nation is in direct ratio to its natural resources. These, as they become known and developed are, in a sense, the central source of motive power which serves to distribute life throughout the whole nation. As goes this source of power, so goes the nation.
While, under our constitution, the administration of the mining industry and certain other resources is a provincial responsibility, the central government still has an important part to play in this regard. It is up to it to foster the use of mining products and others and to ensure their distribution.
Though we might have plenty of oil and other mineral products, they will be of no use to us whatever if we cannot use them, or sell them to others. We should try to process our own raw materials in this country, in so far at least as we are in a position to absorb the finished product.
A greater and more exacting population, together with growing industrialization, will gradually achieve that result for us. In all fairness, however, we must admit that, if part of our primary products are exported as raw materials because they can be more economically processed abroad, the converse is also true. It is as raw material that we import bauxite from South America to process it into aluminum in Canada, thanks to our hydro-electric power. I am sure that all members have heard of Kitimat, in British Columbia, and of Arvida and Comeau Bay in Quebec, so I need not labour the point. Be that as it may, a realistic export policy is absolutely necessary both for our surplus raw materials and for our manufactured


products. That was the policy of the Liberal party and it will again be its policy when it is called upon to preside over the destinies of this country.
Divine Providence willed it that Canada and the United States complete each other geographically. Of our five natural geographical areas, four are closely linked with four identical areas in the neighbouring country. Our economic exchanges take place, therefore, in a north-south and south-north direction. To some extent, this condition may be modified but must never be ignored nor unduly interfered with. The efforts of any Canadian government which, through sentimentality, bravado, naivety or incompetence, ignores the requirements of that geographical situation will be useless, and doomed to failure. Some recent and unhappy events are a convincing proof of it. Since the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Liberal party has succeeded in harmoniously developing our economic relations with the United States while maintaining the integrity of our territory and our institutions. Once again, it will devote itself to that task when, very soon now, the Canadian people will bring it back to power.
Thanks to God, the natural resources of Canada are tremendous. Whether we like it or not, they represent a stake for which the free nations and the rest of the world are competing. If we know how to use them for the benefit of mankind by trying hard to fill the granaries and storehouses of the nations that are deprived of life's barest necessities, we shall not have to use them for stocking up their arsenals and furbishing their weapons. Communism and its despots will always be helpless when faced with the wealth and happiness that every human being has the right to hope for in this world. The hon. members sitting on this side of the house have already made up their mind in this respect. (Text):

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) with great interest.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: If the minister would like to permit the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Christian), who wishes to speak on the same subject-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I wish to speak on the same subject, also.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I am perfectly free to speak, since I will not be closing the debate.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: You must speak on the same grievance.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
Have you a grievance?

V.S. Tariff on Base Metals

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
As I said, I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the members who have spoken on this subject. Coming as I do originally from the Kootenay country in British Columbia, which was opened up as a silver, lead, zinc mining district, in fact I date back a long time farther than either of the members for the Kootenays in that district because I happened to be born there. Always, of course, the residents of that part of British Columbia have been vitally interested in what has been done with silver, lead and zinc. I can assure the hon. members representing the Kootenay district that the present government is just as vitally concerned as they are about this question. They need not think for a minute that they have to convince us that Canada should take a stand with regard to this suggestion that there should be a lead-zinc tariff imposed by the United States.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) outlined very clearly what has been done, and what will be done, when he answered a question on this subject on Saturday last, to be found at page 3455 of Hansard. There he pointed out that a note had been sent to Washington within less than a month of the time that the new government took over, namely on July 19, and he promised that the note would be tabled and the answer thereto just as soon as the formality of clearing with Washington had been gone through. He also pointed out that there had been subsequent discussions on more than one occasion, and even as recently as in December.
We shall certainly take every possible step to persuade our United States friends that they should not impose this tariff. However, as hon. members in all parties of the house know, this is a decision which will be taken by the congress of the United States, and frequently that congress has ignored requests of the kind which have already been made by the present government and has gone merrily on to impose those restrictions which hamper Canadian industries. I know that every member of the house is thoroughly well aware of this fact.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Is it not true that under the procedures of the United States the president can veto any legislation in this regard, and I am hoping that representations will be made in person.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
Yes, I believe it is true that the president could veto any such measure, and I would hope that he will take that step if congress should see fit to impose this duty. But it would be unfortunate if the Canadian people got the impression that all that had to be
done was for some members of the opposition parties in the house to convince the Canadian government that the imposition of the duties should not be permitted. We all know that no government, no matter what its complexion, can ensure that the United States congress would not take this action which will be detrimental to Canada's interests. I can assure the hon. members who have raised this question that we shall not be hesitant in making Canada's position clearly known.
I understand the hon. member for Ville-neuve went a little bit further. He suggested that such metals as lead and zinc should be manufactured right in Canada to a much greater extent and then said that the fact that a Conservative government had come into power was the reason we were having trouble with the United States now about lead and zinc. I should like to point out to him that this threat to our lead and zinc industry dates back a long time before the election. I have here a newspaper dispatch from Washington dated May 25, 1957 and headed, "United States Lead-Zinc Policy Hints at Tariff Boost". It goes on to set out the aim of those people in the United States who wish to have this tariff imposed and has this to say:
As one means of aiding the United States zinc and lead mining industries when the price of the metals drops below certain levels the program would provide for imposition of new import excise taxes in addition to existing tariffs.
It would be interesting to know whether the Liberal government sent any note to Washington or made any protests about this threatened action or just what steps they did take. You see, Mr. Speaker, now in 1958 the Liberals have to answer for what they were doing or not doing seven or eight months ago. They were sitting over here a year ago. They were sitting over here when this question first came up and they had just as much responsibility as we have now, and perhaps a little more, for seeing that this question was dealt with in such a manner as to preserve the rights of the Canadian people. When the hon. member suggests that this problem has arisen now because of a change of government-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, if the minister will permit me, I think he misunderstood what I said. First of all, I did not mention lead and zinc in particular. I was talking about all our natural resources and more particularly about our mining resources. When I said that we should process those resources here in Canada I said that we should process as much as we could absorb and should do everything possible to export the surplus production of our mining resources. I did not blame the

U.S. Tariff on Base Metals government at all for whatever restrictions on exportation of our mining products have come into effect lately. I said it was very unfortunate that there were some restrictions on export. I also said that whatever is being done by the United States is very important. I think the minister misunderstood what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I am glad that was the stand taken by the hon. member. He mentions the wisdom of manufacturing these metals here in Canada to the greatest extent possible and exporting any surplus. As he knows, that has been the policy of the Conservative party since the time of Sir John A. Macdonald and it is one of the basic policies of the Conservative party in Canada today under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: It is the policy of the Liberal party too.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: But it has not been the policy of his own party.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Definitely.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
They have been far more
interested in building up the exportation of raw materials from Canada and the importation of manufactured goods than they have been in having our natural products fabricated here at home.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Will the minister tell me what is the total yearly consumption and the total yearly production of zinc in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I do not have those figures with me at the moment. But actually here is one of the great fundamental differences between the two parties. The Conservative party favours the fabrication of our own raw materials in Canada to the largest extent possible, thereby giving Canadians the first chance to use their own resources and giving Canadians the chance to get jobs in turning their raw materials into finished goods. But that has not been where the emphasis has been placed by the Liberal party down through the years and that is not where the emphasis was placed by the Liberal party in the debate yesterday and today and throughout this whole session. They just do not think along those lines.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: We never sent a junket to Britain at the taxpayers' expense to buy manufactured goods that should be made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I have here a speech by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe to the women's Canadian club on December 3, 1956.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
Is
that a confidential document?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
He set out the Liberal policy very clearly in these words:
-as you know, Canada finds it economical to produce large surpluses of raw materials and foodstuffs with which to pay for the large quantities of imported produce and manufactured goods.
In the same speech he also said:
-Canada is the largest import market in the world for manufactured goods-
Well, the Conservative party of Canada has no ambition to keep Canada the largest import market in the world for manufactured goods-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: You are reducing trade, reducing prosperity.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: We are talking against tariffs, not for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: -especially when it means sending our raw materials to the United States to be fabricated by their workmen and then bought back by the Canadian people.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Do you want us to keep our lead and zinc market? Will the minister permit a question? Does the minister know that of the lead and zinc we produce only about 25 per cent is consumed in Canada and that if we do not export it the whole industry will be closed down? We are talking against tariffs, not for tariffs.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I know that only too well but I am pointing out that the hon. member for Villeneuve is complaining that there should be more fabricating of Canadian metals in Canada. That has not been the policy of the Liberal party, and for the last few weeks I have been amused in listening to the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) get up and complain about this position when all the time the policy of his party has been the policy-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Of expanding trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: -which was enunciated by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe; in other words, to export raw materials and buy back finished goods.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Would he explain to me if this junket, paid for by the taxpayers, to Britain was to buy manufactured goods or raw materials?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) need not try to draw any red herring across the trail. He is very

adept at doing things of that kind. Whenever we get them in a corner on this subject then they start shouting about something over there.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: I am doing the talking now. You keep still for the moment. We have just sat back and listened to this sort of-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: -claptrap long enough. May I point out to the hon. member for Villeneuve that if he really believes in this policy of fabricating raw materials in Canada to the largest extent possible and then exporting the surplus he should be over here with us as a Conservative. He is in the wrong camp. Our friends across the way are never going to get very far in reaching the objective which he has in mind. They seem to think that-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question, and this is not claptrap? Does the insistence of the minister on the fact that we are importing too many manufactured goods mean that the Conservative party is now thinking seriously of returning to its old policy of high tariffs?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: There, Mr. Speaker, is another bright red herring dragged in with a great deal less skill than that shown by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: You have avoided answering with even greater skill. You are an eel, not a red herring.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: These hon. members in the Liberal party, now that they are such big, bold, brave fellows, they want us-

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: -as does the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), to talk up to the United States; to go down and talk to the president.

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: The minister has two minutes to answer two questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: They want us to go down and tell President Eisenhower what he is to do. This is really all very funny. These boys have become so brave, now that they are over in opposition where they cannot do anything. When they were over here such action was the very last thing they would have done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
I do suggest, Mr. Speaker, they should at least be consistent.
U.S. Tariff on Base Metals

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Perhaps the minister could now answer the two questions that were asked.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: At the moment, I cannot tell whether we are at the ante-vote debate or whether we are just winding up. I am not even sure who has the floor. Has the minister completed his remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) want to speak on the same subject?

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I had not intended saying anything on this subject, but I was wondering whether or not the government, in their protest as they call it, had given consideration to the fact that Canadians have bought goods from the United States to the tune of over $1 billion? Instead of sending protests in box car sized letters, possibly the United States might be prevailed upon to believe that it would seem only reasonable that if they want to sell this amount of goods they should take something back from us such as our lead and zinc.
I do not know what the government said in their protests. I would think, however, if we approached the United States government on a reasonable basis, because trade is a twoway street, we would get a lot farther than by making long speeches and sending big protests in box car size letters telling the United States what we are going to do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Is the house agreed that I call it ten o'clock?

maintopic: TRADE-PROPOSED UNITED STATES TARIFF ON BASE METALS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: May I ask the leader of the house what the business is for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Tomorrow, we shall commence with item No. 6 on today's order paper, the second reading of a bill to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities. If that should be finished, then instead of going on with citizenship and immigration estimates, as I mentioned last Monday, we shall take the estimates of the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I wonder if the house leader would give some indication of the business for the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: No, I am sorry-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: We have now reached the point where, according to the house leader's own estimate, the session is drawing to a close. I saw some time ago where it was the intention to move at a later date that Monday and Tuesday mornings be taken away from the house and, that being the case, I think there should be some indication of what they intend to take up during the remainder of this week.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: If the agricultural bill should go through tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, then we would be taking, or I think we would be taking, estimates for the rest of the week. Citizenship and immigration would go on on Thursday and then it would be national revenue after that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Could the minister give any indication of what estimates would be considered on Friday and Saturday?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: My hon. friends say "Oh, oh", but it has been the practice earlier in the session to give the business for the whole week-

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It never was the
practice before.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: -and in earlier sessions as well, but we have not had more than one or two days' notice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Funny how practices came in during this last year.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
You always got the
business one week in advance.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) has been away digging the St. Lawrence seaway for the past several years and he has not known what has been going on. The fact is that the opposition parties this year have had as much notice as we ever had when we were in opposition and I will give them just as much information as I know myself.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: We want more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, the position in the Canadian House of Commons in this present year is somewhat unusual and one would have to be both a prophet and the son of a prophet to give the business of the house for one week ahead. I can assure him and the members of the other parties that I will let them know as much ahead as I know myself. In the meantime they have the information for the next three days, and probably sufficient information for the next four days, which I think is really not doing too badly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although the St. Lawrence seaway is the greatest international program ever undertaken between two neighbouring countries-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: No speeches, please.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: -I suggest that has nothing to do with the question. Whether I was here or not has absolutely nothing to do with the question I asked and I would have thought the hon. gentleman would have co-operated to the extent of giving us the business for the rest of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. member for Laurier feels I am not co-operative.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: May I ask a question of the house leader? In view of his desire to get on with the estimates has consideration been given to referring Bill No. 237 to the committee on agriculture after we have had second reading so that here in the house we can get on with the estimates?

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: A good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: That, Mr. Speaker, sounds like a very tempting offer, but I think everybody, including the hon. member, knows that it is not and the government has no such intention.
